maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SECRETARY GENERAL OP NATO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while I realize that there is never anyone in the galleries, I believe the house will allow me to refer to the fact that we have with us today Paul-Henri Spaak, secretary general of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SECRETARY GENERAL OP NATO
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SECRETARY GENERAL OP NATO
speechtext: The reception accorded those words of mine indicates the feeling that Canadians have for the secretary general of an organization which stands as a bulwark against the spread of Sovietism throughout Europe and indeed throughout the world. I am sure the house would want me to refer to his presence and assure him that Canadians are strongly and unalterably dedicated to the principles of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SECRETARY GENERAL OP NATO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a very special pleasure that I rise to support what the Prime Minister has been good enough to say about our distinguished visitor, both on behalf of my party and on my own behalf. I have had the pleasure of working with Mr. Spaak and I know from first hand, as does the Prime Minister, what he has meant for the development of European and Atlantic unity. Indeed, no man has made a greater contribution to that measure of European unity which has been reached, and no man has done more to extend the concept of European unity across the Atlantic.
Perhaps the best tribute we can pay to the greatness of his Atlantic vision is to work in our respective parliaments toward this realization.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF SECRETARY GENERAL OP NATO
speechtext:
We in the C.C.F. group wish to associate ourselves with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in welcoming our distinguished guest, Paul-Henri Spaak. In addition to his present important position, in the past he
has had a very distinguished political career in his native country. Belgium and Canada have been very closely united in years gone by in a mutual struggle on behalf of democracy and freedom.
We look forward to the development of NATO in the direction of economic co-operation, both among European nations themselves and in the broader north Atlantic community. We think that a greater emphasis on the peaceful purposes and the economic purposes of NATO would be a service to the nations concerned and to mankind in general.

I will go along with that and not get into any general debate on Indian affairs in order to expedite the passage of these estimates. I should like to ask the minister if she could tell me what is the policy of the Indian affairs branch with regard to housing for Indians in the Northwest Territories, particularly as that policy covers the building of log or frame houses. I have nothing against the department's program. As a matter of fact, all I have is praise for the department's program on housing in the Northwest Territories.
However, there are some aspects of this program of which I am critical, and of which the people up there are critical. Why is it that in areas in which there is good timber, good logs for housing, the department builds frame houses, while in other areas where the timber is not good for building log houses the department asks the Indians to haul out fourth and fifth grade logs to put into housing? I wish the minister would tell me whether there is any definite policy on this. Why do they build log houses where they have no logs, and why do they build frame houses where they have plenty of logs?

Mr. Chairman, in general, the type of construction is a matter of agreement with the Indians. I do not know this specific case to which the hon. member refers. If he would be good enough to give me the location and the details I should be happy to get him a complete report. Furthermore, if we find that the proper material has not been used, I can assure him we will look into the matter.

For the residents of Fort Smith, next to Wood Buffalo park where the department of northern affairs claim there is a billion feet of good standing timber, the Indian affairs branch is building frame houses; whereas at Fort Franklin, where there is practically no timber, they are asking the Indians to haul logs to build cabins. At Fort Simpson, where there are plenty of suitable building logs, they build frame dwellings, while in Fort Good Hope, where there are no logs, they are asking the Indians to haul logs for building. There are many other cases about which I will speak to the minister at some other time.
I would also like the minister to tell me what is the general policy with regard to Indian housing. The building of some of these houses is let out on contract. In other places the Indians are asked to provide the labour and the logs to build them. I would also like the hon. lady to give me some information about the new town site at Inuvik where the department of northern affairs erected some 100 buildings. I understand they
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration are turning some of these over for sale to the Indians, but the Indian pays $25 a month rent and the rest goes toward the purchase price of the house. The Indians cannot understand how they can buy and rent at the same time.
Does the hon. member mean they are paying $50 a month?

Fifty dollars a month, of which $25 goes against the purchase of the house and $25 is applied as rent. The Indian would like to purchase a house. He does not see why the whole $50 he pays should not be applied against the purchase price.

I do not have the particulars of the case which the hon. member has brought up, but I think this is a rental purchase scheme. I shall be glad to look into it, but it is probably arranged on the same basis as any other rental purchase agreement.
With regard to the other question the hon. member asked, the policy of the department with respect to housing is that the Indian, if he can, contributes to the erection of his own house either in cash, if he has cash either of his own or from the band fund, or through his own labour. Sometimes a man is fully employed, or employed part time, and would prefer to contribute in cash rather than in labour. In other cases where he is not otherwise engaged he would prefer to be working on the house himself. We think it is very important that the Indian should contribute his share of the cost of the house.
Of course the number of houses built depends on the arrangement made with the band. The band itself decides where the houses are needed most. The band knows approximately how many can be constructed in its own area in a given season, and decides who shall have the houses and what contribution is to be made. There is no hard and fast rule that so much is contributed in all cases either in cash or labour; it is a flexible arrangement between the department and the band council, and the Indian is definitely expected to contribute his share toward the house.

The minister in her reply mentioned co-operation between the agent and the Indians in deciding who is to get a house, and I agree that this does go on. But we have a serious problem raised by the very old people and people who are infirm. For instance, when I last went into Fort Good Hope there were five houses to be built. No one knew when the housing program would start. I went to the tent of a man who was over 70 years of age. He was crippled, and his wife had practically to carry him to the trap line. She did the trapping. I
5068	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration asked this man whether he was getting a house, and he told me he was not. I asked him why and his reply was "I am too old". So I went to see the chief and asked him what was the idea. I told him the man was suffering and that he presumably needed a house, one of the five houses allotted. But the chief said "He is too old. If we build a new house he will not live that long." The young people ask why these houses should go to the very old and to people who are only going to live a very short length of time.
This brings up another problem, the problem of homes for the aged and infirm. In the past four or five years both Roman Catholic and Anglican missions have closed down a number of schools and will be closing down hospitals this year at Aklavik. Hospitals and schools have already been closed at Fort Providence and Resolution. I feel the department should give serious consideration to using these buildings as homes for the aged and infirm, and also as means of relieving another serious problem, that of Indian children who are left to fend for themselves after both parents have been taken from home, possibly to enter a tuberculosis hospital. I really think the minister should give consideration to providing one such home at Fort Providence, one at Resolution and at least one at Aklavik to look after this situation.

As the hon. member says, these are very real problems. I hope the opening of the new regional office at Fort Smith, which I discussed in the committee yesterday, will lead to more adequate supervision of the area. This question of housing for aged persons is another problem, of course. I remember that last summer when I was at Winterburn, west of Edmonton, the band there had set up an old people's community. They had about six houses, and an aged couple was living in each. They were nice little houses and everyone was most happy about it. I am sure the old people themselves were happier than they would have been in an institution.
This problem also requires the co-operation of the band. I do not think the department could move in over the head of the band unless action was taken on an institutional basis and you removed the people from the band and put them in an institution. Again the human element arises, and whether they would want to go is another problem.
I can assure the hon. member that we are looking into this problem. This is one of the matters that have to be faced, and I hope we can come up with a solution concerning what to do about these aged persons.

The minister announced the establishment of a new regional office in Fort Smith. I am very happy that over the past few years an increasing number of people have been placed in the north by the Indian affairs branch to look after the welfare of the native peoples. However, the progress has been too slow, and we need additional people. In a speech I made in this chamber some years ago I pointed out that there were 23 game wardens in the area I represent and four people working for the Indian affairs branch. In other words there were 23 people looking after the welfare of game and only four looking after the welfare of human beings. The department is still not doing enough, and more men should be put in the field.
Every day I receive letters from places like Snowdrift, where they have not seen an Indian agent for months. It is not the fault of the agent, who has too large an area to cover. Assistant Indian agents should be placed in isolated places such as Snowdrift, Fort Providence and Fort Liard. At Fort Rae we have the largest settlement of Indians in the Northwest Territories, but there is no Indian agent or assistant.
We are told that we have less game, including caribou, than we ever had, but the population of native Indians is increasing. If the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources can sell treasury board on the idea of hiring game wardens and forestry people, a good many of whom are stationed at places where there is no timber, there is no reason why the Indian affairs branch cannot convince treasury board of the genuine need for an increase in staff to look after the human element in our part of the country.

National gallery of Canada-
240. Administration, operation and maintenance including grants as detailed in the estimates, $929,145.

Mr. Chairman, this year the national gallery of Canada entered upon a new era of its history. In November, 1959 the entire national collection and the personnel maintaining it moved from the old premises in the Victoria memorial museum to the new Lome building on Elgin street in central Ottawa. The move was a highly specialized operation requiring the skilled and careful handling of priceless works of art, a voluminous library, valuable scientific equipment and office furnishing. Thanks to very ably co-ordinated direction I am happy to state that the move was successfully completed without accident, loss or incident of any kind.
The new national gallery of Canada was opened by the Prime Minister, Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, before a distinguished gathering of some 3,000 persons on Wednesday evening, February 17, 1960.
All in white ties.

Congratulatory addresses were presented by representatives of museum associations in Europe, the United States and Canada. The occasion was further celebrated by an inaugural loan exhibition of old master paintings, generously and willingly lent by many of the great national collections of the western world.
I am happy to report, too, that since that gala opening evening the national gallery of Canada has established a record of unprecedented attendance. Beginning on February 17 and ending as of the closing hour on June 16, the checked attendance has been 299,163 persons. If modesty did not prevent me from doing so perhaps I could give some of that information to the committee myself, but I prefer to have it come officially from the minister.
I must say that it was a great satisfaction to me personally, and I think it was a great satisfaction to all members of the previous administration who authorized the building of the new national gallery and who made every arrangement for it, to see the completion of this great project which they had planned, organized and started.
I must say that on the occasion of that gala white-tie opening by the Prime Minister I was not altogether surprised to be asked by one of those present a question to which I did not know the answer in the context in which it was asked. That question was, "What do we have a governor general for?" The question was put because when the original national gallery was opened in the 1880's it was opened by the Marquis of Lome, who at that time was governor general of Canada. It would have appeared to some of us that this was an occasion of sufficient consequence to have warranted the appearance at that time of the representative of the crown; but I do not intend to labour that point at all.
There are certain unfortunate circumstances that did attend that opening. The most unfortunate of all, I think, was that the man who perhaps had done more than any other person, by his hard work and his enthusiasm, to get the kind of support for the gallery which it now enjoys in this country was not present. I refer to Mr. Alan Jarvis, who "retired" from the position of director shortly before the opening of the gallery. In all the speeches that were made on that occasion his name was not even mentioned. It did seem to me that this was not the kind of generosity, and even good sense,


that there ought to have been on a nonpartisan occasion of this kind on the part of the government of our country.
I do not blame the government for not mentioning the fact that it was the government of Mr. St. Laurent that was responsible for this project. One can understand why they did not mention that. There was the barest mention of the fact that Mr. Percy Fell also had something to do with it but he was at least present. Outside of that it was, it seemed to me, an example of conscious or unconscious partisanship or a sort of private possession on the part of a political party in the government of our country that I think is to be deplored on occasions of that kind. I feel that this ought to be said, not because what was done can be undone but in the hope that this kind of partisan exploitation of the common possessions of all the Canadian people will not happen again.
Now, sir, I do want to say a word or two about some of the unfortunate things that I think have happened in connection with the administration of the national gallery. I think it is very unfortunate that the gallery lost the services of Mr. Jarvis. I do not think that anyone who did not have the experience I had and the experience that some of my colleagues had can calculate the effect of Mr. Jarvis' enthusiasm and drive in creating in this country a support for the national gallery and a public interest in it on the part of all sorts and conditions of people that was really extraordinary. Those very gratifying figures that the minister gave up to the latest date, which I think was last night, of 300,000 people who had already visited the gallery since it opened is, I think, some evidence of the kind of public interest there is in the national gallery and in the arts in this country today.
I do think, too, that it would not be fitting tc refer on this occasion to this development without making a reference to the former governor general of Canada, Right Hon. Vincent Massey, who in every capacity that he has had throughout the course of his distinguished adult life has been a great and discerning patron of the arts, and who, in the contribution he made to those things which are more than bread alone, through the report of his commission and through the other interest he has shown in this matter, should not be forgotten on an occasion of this kind. Indeed, if the government had chosen to invite Mr. Massey to open the national gallery I do not think anyone would have felt that it was a misplaced tribute.
I do not intend to make any great issue- because I am sure Mr. Jarvis does not want any great issue made-of the circumstances of

his retirement. I do not want to say anything unnecessary about other aspects, other unfortunate incidents, that have occurred in the past year. But there are one or two things that it is necessary, in my opinion, to say. The retirement of so distinguished a citizen as Mr. Cleveland Morgan from the board of the national gallery took place in a fashion which caused the Montreal Gazette-which is, I think, normally pretty friendly to the present government and certainly pretty friendly to the party that the present government represents in this house-to say this in an editorial on October 26. The editorial is headed "Too Much Interference" and goes on to say:
It may become increasingly difficult for the government to find good and qualified citizens to serve on independent boards and tribunals, if the government insists on interfering with their policies and decisions.
The latest example of the sort of troubles that are arising is seen in the resignation of Mr. F. Cleveland Morgan of Montreal from the board of trustees of the national gallery of Canada. His resignation follows that of another trustee of the gallery, Mr. C. P. Fell of Toronto.
I am not going to put the rest of the editorial on Hansard. I think it is only characteristic of the difference between their personalities, but not characteristic of the difference in their attitude to the government, that at the time Mr. Morgan resigned Mr. Lawren Harris, who is not only one of the greatest of our artists but a man of extraordinary discernment and capacity in many fields, and who has made a great contribution as a member of the board of the national gallery, also had something to say, and I have here a news clipping from the Vancouver Sun of October 29. It is headed "Harris Adds Voice to Gallery Uproar", and reads as follows:
Vancouver, Oct 28 (CP)-Artist Lawren Harris today added his voice to protests against the federal government appointment of a new chairman of the national art gallery without reference to the trustees. Mr. Harris, a trustee of the gallery for several years, also said the government "hasn't taken any interest at all" in the gallery.
F. Cleveland Morgan of Montreal resigned from the board of trustees in protest against the appointment of Thomas Maher of Quebec city as chairman without consultation with the board. Mr. Harris, however, said he will not resign from the board.
"I think it would be a mistake to resign," he said. "If you resign, you're out. You can't say anything. I'll stay until they force me out."
Mr. Harris added that art dealers all over the world now are suspicious of deals with the Canadian gallery because of the federal government's reversal of a decision to buy a painting by Lorenzo Monaco.
"The government told us to go ahead and a London art dealer bought the painting. Then the government turned around and refused to buy it. This would never have happened with a Liberal government," he said.

I was interested in the opening of the gallery, which ceremony I attended in a black tie; but I think the arrangements showed that someone was a little out of touch with the needs and interests of the people in general, when provision was made for attendance by 5,000 people wearing white ties. A whole brigade of people wearing white ties; imagine that. What a frightening prospect in connection with the national gallery. Anyone would think it was a military parade. While I understand the symbolic nature of the white tie I think it could have been confined to the few, to the inner group of very important people. Therefore I suggest that in future invitations to these functions should be given out in a way which would not prohibit the attendance of a large number of ordinary people who are artists or interested in art.
Let me point out first, that it would be impossible to obtain 5,000 white ties in Ottawa at one time for one function; and second, that the great majority of those who are interested in the art gallery cannot afford an outfit of this style. I do suggest that an opportunity be provided on other occasions for ordinary people like the hon. member for Kootenay West to attend, in ordinary clothes.

I had made up my mind to say this, and I will do so. I thought it was the most shocking example of bad manners on the part of the people in the white tie class that I have ever seen in my life. speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I submitted the estimates of my department last year, I pointed out that the mining industry had just gone through its first recession since the end of world war II. However, the drop in production for 1958 was not a serious one. Yet I indicated that prospects were already better and that in 1959, we could expect a good year.
Before continuing with the estimates of my department, I am happy to tell you that, last year, our mining production exceeded all former records, reaching a value of 2.4 billion dollars, and this trend has been maintained for most significant minerals since the beginning of 1960.
I would now like to say a few words about certain aspects of the situation of our mining industry which are especially significant and stimulating. I shall also list some important steps taken by my department, which are
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys meant to further the development of Canada's huge mineral resources to a still greater extent.
(Text):
In the early part of 1959 the Canadian mineral industry was operating at levels considerably below capacity. A decline in industrial activity, and a condition of surplus mineral stocks in the United States had been important contributing factors to this situation. However, as the year moved on mineral demand improved with the general economic expansion in both North America and Europe. Strikes in the steel and nonferrous metals industries in the United States during the second half of 1959 also resulted in an increased demand for Canadian minerals. As a result of all of these and other factors iron ore shipment rose sharply, nickel output registered marked increases, and such other minerals as copper and asbestos came into greater demand.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, during the latter part of 1959 the over-all improvement in our mineral situation was general, with the exceptions of coal, uranium, lead and zinc. The coal industry has, of course, been experiencing considerable difficulties in recent years, and this matter is currently receiving the careful attention of a royal commission. The adverse decision of the United States atomic energy authority in November with respect to the renewal of Canadian contracts after 1962 has meant a considerable adjustment in the uranium industry. This matter is under continuing study, as you will have noted from statements of my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I am pleased to report that conditions in the lead and zinc industry have improved in recent months following the depressed market situation which existed from 1957 well into 1959. The United Nations lead and zinc study group, in which Canada is well represented, has been carrying on a continuing study of the world situation in lead and zinc and the 25 members of the group have held several important meetings to discuss mutual problems relative to world surpluses. Canadian lead and zinc producers are naturally encouraged by the recent improvement in market conditions because over 80 per cent of their production is sold on the export market. They do, however, still face uncertainties relative to a report of the United States tariff commission to be made in October of this year.
With few exceptions, Canadian mineral commodities have experienced favourable growth situations since the latter part of 1959 as a result of their generally improved position in world markets, particularly in the
5088	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys United States and the United Kingdom. Although the export market remains of paramount importance for the mineral industry in general, there is a progressive increase in demand for iron ore, copper, lead, fuels and industrial minerals in the domestic market. In fact, I believe a related development of considerable significance to the mineral industry and the economy at large is under way with respect to the increasing trend toward greater mineral processing in Canada.
I could illustrate this by referring to several mining developments which have been of first importance during the past year. At Thompson, Manitoba, the International Nickel Company's new mining project is proceeding on schedule and is expected to come into full production next year at an annual rate of 75 million pounds of nickel. This operation will be second only in size to the Sudbury area in terms of world nickel production and all of its ore will be refined to nickel metal at a new refinery now being constructed at Thompson.
The Coronation mine in Saskatchewan and the Chisel lake mine in Manitoba are being brought into production this year and the copper concentrates from these new mines will be smelted and refined to metal in Canadian smelters and refineries. The Montreal east copper refinery, the second largest in the world, is being expanded to a capacity of
270,000	tons per year to handle increased production from the Noranda smelter as well as the output from Murdochville in the Gaspe peninsula and Flin Flon, Manitoba. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited stands ready to bring the large Pine Point deposit on Great Slave lake into production, with the lead-zinc concentrate to be treated at Trail, B.C. The company also will commence a pig iron operation this year at Kimberley, B.C., with initial plans for an orderly expansion up to 1,000 tons of pig iron per day.
Other developments which have contributed to continuing growth and diversification of the Canadian mineral economy during the past year include three large iron ore mining projects in the Quebec-Labrador district, the preparation for zinc mining operations in the Mattagami lake area of northern Quebec, and a country-wide reactivation of a number of smaller base metal mining properties. Petroleum resource development has continued to make its major contribution, particularly in the natural gas sector. The potash industry in Saskatchewan is proceeding toward production. This province stands to become one of the major sources of potash in the world. The base metal deposits in New Brunswick seem to be moving toward the production stage.

branch's work on ground stress, long range program of direct concern to some of our deeper mines, should lead to better mining practices. To speed the development of our iron ore deposits the branch is seeking new and better methods of treating these ores. Its work with industry is well known. Many of the current processes in use in Canadian mining and milling were developed or improved by mines branch research. At a time when some facets of the industry are in difficulty I need not dwell on the importance of this work.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has stressed the need for increased sales of uranium. I might mention here that our mines branch is currently investigating possible new uses for this commodity, one of our most important projects. I pannot, of course, say how successful our efforts will ultimately be; but it has already been established that uranium can be a useful alloying element, particularly for the production of steels of high fatigue strength.
The branch, of course, delves into many other problems. In the study of non-metallic minerals alone a dozen research projects are under way, many of which are of direct benefit to producers of industrial minerals and construction materials. Its work on fossil fuels points to a broader market for coal and improved refining techniques for crude oil. Its work with Canadian producers and fabricators of zinc is leading to new uses, and hence an improved market, for this commodity; and its research in physical metallurgy is bringing about the development of new alloys in urgent demand for missile development and nuclear research. These and many other items have been allowed for in our estimates for the mines branch.
In our estimates we have included $2,042,708 for the dominion observatories. With space research very much to the fore these days a great deal of interest has been focused on this branch of our department. Its work in the past has contributed greatly to the science of astronomy, to the international geophysical year and to many other related projects. The observatories have recently moved into the field of radio astronomy; and on June 20 I shall be pleased to preside at the opening of its new radio telescope at Penticton, British Columbia. This instrument will be used in a full scale study of distant hydrogen clouds and, to some extent, in an investigation of Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and other members of the solar system.
The observatories will be making airborne magnetometer observations over the Arctic islands, the Arctic ocean, in the neighbourhood of the north magnetic pole and over the

north Atlantic. It is also setting up a new network of seismic stations in northern Canada and the Arctic islands.
This year the branch's gravity surveys will be considerably increased to meet the demands of industry and national defence. Observations will be made over the prairies and in many parts of northern Canada.
In Ottawa the mirror transit, a new instrument in astronomic work, will be used to study positions and motions of stars and members of the solar system. In Victoria the 73-inch telescope will be used in the observatories' continuing study of interstellar gases, very hot stars and those of great brightness. The work of the geographical branch will call for the expenditure of $399,833. (Translation):
The publication of the Atlas of Canada, in French as well as in English, is a recent undertaking of the geographical branch. This is hardly the moment to elaborate on the scope of the task involved in the publication of such a work but, in my opinion, we can rightly state that this has been one of the finest achievements of our department. (Text):
This fiscal year the geographical branch will be intensifying its land use surveys. These studies, undertaken in co-operation with the provinces, lay the foundation for planned agriculture, forestry and many other endeavours of importance to the efficient development of our natural resources. The branch will also continue its investigation of ice conditions in the gulf of St. Lawrence and undertake various field studies of importance to our knowledge of Canada's geography.
May I say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that it was not my aim in these remarks to defend the work of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I feel that its record speaks for itself; and I should like to use this occasion to congratulate and thank all the officials and employees of my department for the splendid and efficient work they are doing. The department has over the years been a powerful force in the economic development of this country, and its role in the future will be one of special significance to Canada's continued growth.

Certainly, but this is the point I wish to make. If it were not uranium it would probably be another mineral, but if we could be assured of maintaining our uranium production during the next 10, 15, 20 or 25 years, or even of increasing it, I am sure that the mineral production would keep on rising on a large scale. However, this is my point: I hope that our mining production will keep up at the highest possible level but the marketing of our minerals is becoming increasingly difficult. The United States are more and more difficult and the best example of this is in the case of uranium.
We had contracts with the United States atomic energy authority for the production of uranium until 1962. As a matter of fact,

the United States were so worried about being short of this important product that they pleaded with Canada to give them options on our uranium production from 1962 to 1966 and the companies concerned granted those options.
In due course, the United States decided not to take up those options and, as I said, we should have urged them, at the time, to meet their commitments. I think that in this way we would have got them to take up at least part of these options. I notice that the minister seems to disapprove; but industrialists and mine owners believe that, if Canada had insisted with the United States, we would have succeeded in getting the American government to take at least part of those options, and in that case we would now perhaps be assured of an annual production of $300 or $325 million for the next eight or ten years, instead of an annual production of $250 million for the next four or five years. So much for the matter of uranium.
As far as base metals, like copper and zinc, are concerned, it is well known that the United States, not quite two years ago, introduced a tax of 1.7 cents a pound on copper and they do not seem to be considering the removal of that tax. This tax is a handicap to our copper producers, and it is known what a quota system on zinc means for the industry. Production has to be curtailed; several mines had to close down and others will have to control their production in order not to exceed their quotas. These are problems in which the government must take interest, and perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce should go more often to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys for advice as far as the sale of our metals, either to the United States or to Europe, is concerned.
In fact, we should probably be able to sell base metals to European countries if we had an aggressive team who would study European markets. People are well aware of the complications arising out of the trading agreements of the European countries, known as the Six and the Seven. We should try to approach the representatives of those countries or try to negotiate with them in order to dispose of a greater quantity of our base metals.
I know that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is mostly interested not


only in the production of Canadian metals, but also in their sale. Our domestic consumption takes up only a very small part of our production. Such are the matters on which I would like to call the attention of the minister. And now, Mr. Chairman, concerning the current studies on the polar continental shelf, it should not be forgotten that, in the same field, there are continental shelves adjacent to the provinces too.
I think that certain works have been undertaken. I understood the minister to say that work had been undertaken in the Magdalen islands and that certain projects had also been launched on the coast of New Brunswick and in the gulf of St. Lawrence.
I do not intend to deal at length with this matter now because I want to discuss it in great detail later on, but since it has been made clear in 1958 that the mineral resources of the continental shelf belong to the neighbouring country, I believe the time has come for the federal government to face the situation and to transfer those resources to the provinces, particularly where they are close to the provinces in James bay, in Hudson bay, in the gulf of St. Lawrence and along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. On the other hand, as far as the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island are concerned, I believe that we should transfer to them those natural resources that we find on the continental shelf in a certain radius from those provinces.
I think we should transfer to the province of Quebec the resources found in the continental shelf along the gulf of St. Lawrence, close to the province of Quebec. Further, we should transfer to Newfoundland the part concerning that province, along the Labrador coast and around the island of Newfoundland. As to the sections located in Hudson bay and James bay, we should also transfer the relevant portions to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. On the Pacific coast, such natural resources should be transferred to British Columbia. This is a very important matter. Moreover, we should transfer to the provinces the small islands located along their coasts. This is a problem of great concern to the Canadian people and particularly to the province of Quebec.
I think the minister should consult with his colleagues, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) and even the Prime Minister, and discuss the
17, 1960	5095
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys possibility of transferring the natural resources that are part of the continental shelf to the various provinces along the coast.
I think such action on his part would be highly appreciated not only by the provinces concerned, but by every Canadian. It is a most important matter. Perhaps he will also have an opportunity to discuss this plan with the next premier of the province of Quebec.

I want to add another thing. Since the minister mentioned university research grants through the geological commission, I must say that I think this is a good idea, which will benefit not only the mining industry but the whole country. The grants were introduced quite a long time ago. They have been raised to $50,000, and I quite agree with the minister when he says that they should be increased. They should, in fact, be substantially increased, not because the government is being asked to employ more geologists or because some of them are out of work, but because we have large geological projects to carry out. Indeed, we could double the staff of the Canadian geological commission. We are making no mistake in encouraging a greater number of young men to take up geological studies.
Especially in the summertime, to encourage students.

Especially in the summertime. Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Essex East says that we should encourage students much more. We must give credit to the minister for what he is doing. Last year, many students were jobless. But, as a result of representations made to the department
5096	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys by the geological commission, as well as by the mining industry, the government did employ a greater number of geologists. In view of the slackening tempo of mining operations in private industry, the department was asked to employ a greater number of geologists, and it did so, taking on several young men. I should think that this year a greater number of students will be employed, due to the fact that 88 teams will be at work.
I should like to get more information from the minister about that. Perhaps he might let me have them when we take up the various items of his estimates. Then we will know how many students can be hired for the summer.

Mr. Chairman, the act respecting the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys sets out in seven general subsections of section 6 the further duties of the minister other than the general one to have jurisdiction over mines, minerals, explosives and technical surveys. The scope of his responsibility is very wide. It has been my feeling and observation that the department has never had the interest on the part of the government that it should have had. I think this general attitude was substantiated very strongly by the report published last year by the committee on mines, forests and waters. This very same committee considered the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and came up with the suggestion that forestry should have a larger place. The government has given an indication that it is going to move in the direction that the committee wished by creating a department of forestry.
But while the committee's report on the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources was critical to a degree, its report on the minister's department was the most devastating I have encountered of any report made by a parliamentary committee. I was very interested in it since, along with members who in the main are supporters of


the government, I helped to prepare it. I will not claim that I played a large role but I was certainly in general agreement with many of the criticisms. These criticisms were published in the report of the committee which appeared in the minutes and proceedings of the standing committee last year for May 25.
I expected from the minister some resume of how the department has moved to meet the criticisms expressed in that report. I am not going to be critical of the resume he gave us but with regard to almost every phase of the department's activities there was a critical appraisal in the committee's report. One thing I should like to suggest is that the minister concerned should arrange to have his department reviewed next year not by the committee on mines, forests and waters but by the estimates committee of the House of Commons. In view of the very serious criticisms made last year by a committee that was intimately concerned with the subject matter, it seems to me that we need a further review of the department very soon from the spending point of view and an analysis made on the basis of that approach. I hope the minister will consider doing this because I am going to point out some extremely severe criticism in the recommendations of the committee.
I might add that the year before the very same committee examined the department and made a fourth report which was published on July 31, 1958. The 1958 report was not nearly as critical and the committee, of course, did not go as deeply into the affairs of the department. But recommendation No. 11 in the 1958 report was in these words:
Your committee recommends that the government give consideration to the necessity for increasing the department's research program and facilities in order to keep pace with the accelerated tempo of northern development.
That is about the strongest suggestion in that report, but when you turn to the 1959 report you find nothing but strong suggestions or recommendations. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee the recommendation found in paragraph seven of the committee's report. It is, of course, a reflection on the previous government much more than on the present minister. It reads as follows:
In almost all fields of national scientific endeavour, this department should have led and should lead the way. There is little need for this committee to apportion blame for the present state. Both

the people and those responsible for policy in Canada have been slow to realize the urgent need for expenditure and leadership in this field. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, your committee insists, must be recognized as a vitally important one, not one of inferior significance. The scientific function of the department cannot any longer be circumscribed by caution, hesitancy and lack of support. It is imperative that all branches of the department embark on an accelerated program of expansion, and planning for expansion; and that the provision of the needed money, staff and facilities be an immediate consideration of the government.
Let me tell the minister how pleased I am to see that the estimates for this year have been increased by $5,700,000, but I would have been much happier if I had not found that so much of this increase, as a matter of fact $3J million, is going for the construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment. I realize that before you can expand a research program you need these things but I would have liked to see more of the increase this year devoted to the specific areas of research that the committee recommended. I want to go on to point out to the minister where these areas are. I think that perhaps the best place to start is where the committee's criticism was most severe and that is with the mines branch. In that respect the committee had this to say:
The information elicited on the mines branch was depressing. The branch does not have the funds or the staff it needs to carry out the work it should do and wants to do.
When I check the particulars of the estimates I cannot get any great encouragement that the minister is moving in the light of this particular criticism. Another area of the department that was criticized was the dominion coal board. I should like to draw the minister's attention to this statement.
Your committee learned with regret of losses of coal markets in both western and eastern Canada through a lack of liaison between the coal producer and the consumer. Your committee recommends that every possible effort be made to ensure that this situation is corrected.
If we turn to the geological survey of Canada we find the following in paragraph 55:
It is essential that the geological survey must not only keep pace with the mineral industry, but work ahead of it, providing the industry with geological information well in advance. If this objective is not met the function of the survey is not only seriously impaired but, as well, the information which is eventually supplied by the survey will have been obtained at an excessive cost in relation to the effort expended to obtain it. This has proven to be the fact.
That is a very serious criticism of this branch. We were made aware in the committee, and the committee so reported, that
17, 1960	5097
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys the geography division was short of geographers and that so far as geodesy was concerned we had an almost laughable situation compared with the Americans, although the Americans were very weak and puny compared with the Russians. With respect to the surveys and mapping branch the committee made this recommendation:
-the staff increase in this branch should be progressive over the period of the next five years to facilitate training and to increase assimilation.
The report went on to urge that much greater efforts be made in this particular field. It seems to me this was a call by a House of Commons committee to greater effort on the part of the minister to make his department more important. The reasons for urging this have been well put by the previous speaker. The part of the country from which I come, as the minister may know, totals
148,000	square miles, and this is a considerable chunk of the Laurentian shield. The whole hope for the future growth of this area rests on the development of the metal industry, and specifically the iron ore and base metal industries. It is rather disconcerting, in this particular situation, when you have two jurisdictions. We have a provincial jurisdiction and a federal jurisdiction, and there is very little indication of aggressive leadership in this particular field from either one, that is direct encouragement in the base metal or iron ore development.
I have been wanting to tell the minister how very pleased I was to have the opportunity of looking at these particular reports that have been prepared largely by Mr. R. D. Elver of the mineral resources division. This is the kind of survey of the prospects of the iron ore industry of which we should have more and which should be well broadcast so that the people appreciate the opportunity we have.
I might refer to one of these reports by Mr. Elver which came out in March, 1960, entitled "Direct iron ore processes and their prospects in eastern Canada". This is the kind of thing one welcomes from a department such as this. It is an economic survey of a very concrete situation, with an attempt to assess where we may get expansion, and not the least of my interest in this survey comes from the fact that two places are projected as being likely sources of direct iron industries, one being Seven Islands and the other being Port Arthur. I would suggest to the minister that we could stand many more analyses of this type, and the popularization of these analyses should be made on a fairly wide front.
Here again I should like to congratulate the department upon some of the publications it is putting out in an attempt to popularize the department. I am thinking especially of
5098	HOUSE OF
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys one which was very attractive, the one I have here, which we all received recently. I hope the minister will see that this goes out not only to industry but to regional offices, development associations, chambers of commerce and so on. We are not getting an appreciation of what the department can do.
I must say in this regard that despite my criticism last year I had the opportunity of bringing a sample along certain lines to the minister's officials, and in so far as the assay report was concerned, it was a good economic appreciation. I thought that the reply and service were excellent.
One of the things that concerns me after the mines committee report of last year, and after the statement of the minister, was the fact that the Canadian metal association came out with an argument that they did not want the government to get into any more research. I have not got that particular clipping here, but I know for a fact they particularly did not want the government to get into any more advanced metallurgical research. There was an indication, as I read the comment, which I believe was made by the permanent secretary or secretary manager of that organization, that they felt the industry could take care of its own research in this particular field. The minister is shaking his head, and perhaps I misinterpreted it. I know definitely this was the interpretation I took from the report. I was disappointed in this comment. I hope it will not discourage the department.
I was not aware of that.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Was this criticism of the research a reflection on the national research council?

No, I do not think it was. I think it was specifically a reaction to the indication that this particular department was going to expand its research program. In so far as the national research council is concerned, I may say I knew a young scientist who was working for the minister's department not long ago. He has since moved. I checked, personally, as to why he had moved because he was a friend. It happened to be one of the evenings when the house was not sitting, so he said get in your car and I will show you why. We drove out to one of these old buildings of the mines department, and it was all in darkness. He said, now let us go for a drive out the other way. We went to the national research council building on Sussex street and he said, now look. There were lots of lights on. He showed me another national research council building and there were more lights on. He said, I am so fed up with the business of a scientist in the mines and technical surveys branch being looked upon as


a kind of nine to five job. He said that in the national research council you are given much greater opportunity to work when you possibly can. It is not looked upon as a nine to five job. It is much more exciting; it is much easier to get equipment and have your specifications for an experiment checked. It was for these reasons, this lack of the kind of atmosphere that Dr. Steacie attempts to create in the national research council, perhaps very successfully, that this particular Ph.D. got out of the department. I just mention that to the minister as an indication of the kind of research spirit that needs to prevail in his kind of organization, and to suggest perhaps it does not exist there whereas it could and does in the national research council.
One of the aspects of the department that has been brought into question in my mind relates to its position to other government departments. I might refer in this connection to the uranium industry difficulties. Here we have a mining development that has come a cropper, and come a cropper for perhaps a decade or more. The department that one would think would properly be most concerned with the research aspect and all the other aspects of the problem has had almost nothing to do with it, so far as I know. I do believe it would have been much better, both for the Elliot Lake situation and the situation as a whole, if the minister of mines had been responsible rather than the Minister of Trade and Commerce, even though it may have been a merchandising or marketing problem that fell under that department. Certainly in terms of alternatives, what to do with these uranium properties, certainly in terms of background so far as the mining industry is concerned, it seems to me the mines department had it over trade and commerce.
I think of coal, for example, which is a marketing problem to a degree according to our house committee report. We do not have coal under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I should like to know from the minister what his department is doing in so far as the uranium industry and its future is concerned. Is there any possibility at all of any of the research that is supposedly being rushed to find alternative uses for uranium originating in his department? Could his department play any role at all in this matter?
One of the specific questions that I wanted to ask the minister was the relationship of his department to the department of northern affairs in so far as this roads to resources program is concerned. As I understand it, one particular mining group in my constituency has a prospect into which they hope to put a fair amount of money. As a

matter of fact, I believe their development program calls for something in excess of $1 million. They applied, and were supported as I understand in their application by nearby communities, to have one of the roads put in partly sponsored by federal funds. I take it from the reply of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the road was turned down and the basis for the turndown was an adverse report on the prospects of this particular property or company or development from the minister's department. I cannot be critical of the turndown because it may have been a proper one, but I should like to know how the information was gathered on this particular matter. In this case, since there so much expectation in our region and so much disappointment over the failure of the road program to go through, I think we would appreciate a full explanation.
The area in economic research which I should especially like to recommend to the minister is the future market for our iron ore in so far as it relates to Europe and the whole prospects of the kind of program that Cyrus Eaton had in contemplation in so far as Greenland, Germany and other parts of Europe are concerned. One of the difficulties for the ordinary member of the public, so far as mining is concerned, is the continual launching or the promotion of gigantic schemes-one might almost call them dreams -of developments here and developments there, assuming parts of Canada are always next year country or next decade country, not a little owing to the promotional imagination of people in the mining field. I think the kind of sober, thorough assessment that we should have here could be done on a wider scale and bring a bit more realism into this particular picture.
Another point I wanted to refer to was touched upon by the hon. member for Villeneuve, namely the question of jurisdiction or actual ownership of the continental shelf. I think the minister is aware of the fact that the regulations promulgated by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in so far as oil exploration is concerned, as I understand them, indicate that the federal government has decided to claim that jurisdiction. I have not any quarrel with this decision. It is regrettable to me and to my associates that a number of our natural resources were allowed to lapse, especially in the thirties, by the provinces; but I would appreciate from the minister a statement in this regard especially from the point of view of what consideration the government is giving. Were the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and the officials
17, 1960	5099
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys who are carrying out continental shelf projects and surveys consulted before the minister of northern affairs came out with these regulations? Is there any indication that the provinces are objecting to this particular approach? If so, generally what are the views of the minister and his officials on the matter? It seems to me this is a most legitimate point to have brought out.
The question of the geological survey and its relationship to students has been covered by the minister to a degree. Several years ago he gave me a reply that indicated there was a limited role the department could play in so far as the undergraduate is concerned. This particular summer is a very hard one on university students, just as was the one two years ago. It was an especially hard one two years ago, as the minister will recall, for students in geology. I wonder what consideration the minister has given to making a more flexible program that may be able to adjust quickly to a developing situation such as that which is upon us this summer when there is a great shortage of opportunities for many students in fields that relate to mining. I am thinking not only of geology but of mining engineering and other fields such as geography and the like, where students can get an exceptionally good part of their training in working on these particular surveys.
We have every reason to be prouder, I think, of the geological survey than of any other branch of the Canadian government. I think a case could be made for the proposition that it has been the most important and the best section of government in almost any real terms in our Canadian history. It is certainly the oldest of the scientific branches and it has made a contribution to the development of Canada that no one can really get into good focus, not the least because of these promotional extravangazas and the tendency to build up our mining picture historically upon the basis of types like Sir Harry Oakes. Long before Sir Harry Oakes, Gilbert LaBine and people like them were abroad in the land they had these geological teams far ahead, sometimes 50 and 60 years ahead.
We were talking a few weeks ago about Red Lake and the coming back of certain mines there. Robert Bell, a very distinguished man from Queen's University, in 1872 and 1873 was up in the Red Lake mining area long before the railroad was put through there and spotted these green stone formations on which the Howey camp developed. He also spotted the greenstone formation in lake Minnitaki that runs down through Atikokan on which many of our other best deposits have come along.

Mr. Speaker,
I wish to raise three points in connection with this case to which I think serious consideration should be given. The first is an

Private Bills-Divorce
examination as to whether there was a marriage and if so should that marriage be dissolved. The second point concerns an examination as to whether there is proper domicile within a province which would allow this bill to be presented to parliament. If there is not proper domicile it may be determined that parliament has no jurisdiction. The third point concerns an examination of the basis on which dissolution of the marriage is sought. Adultery is alleged and we must examine whether adultery took place. The committee of the other place and the other chamber itself has dealt with the bill and passed it through its various stages.
Because this is the first occasion on which I have a recollection of your being in the chair, Mr. Speaker, during a discussion on second reading of divorce bills, perhaps I should state that I seek permission to follow my usual practice of refraining from mentioning the names and addresses of the people involved in this case.
The petition reads as follows:
The petition of-
Giving the name of the petitioner.
-teacher, of the city of Toronto, province of Ontario,
Humbly Sheweth:	.
1. That your petitioner was lawfully married to-
Giving the name of the respondent.
-on or about the 7th day of September, A.D. 1954, at the city of Toronto, province of Ontario, your petitioner's maiden name being-presently residing at-
Giving the address.
__in the city of Toronto, province of Ontario,
with her parents-
Giving their names.
-and your petitioner, moreover, was never married before her marriage to the respondent herein.
The petitioner under oath produced documentary evidence as proof of her marriage. The marriage took place in Toronto but the evidence reveals that the respondent has always been domiciled in Montreal. I submit that we have jurisdiction to deal with divorce from any province of Canada on any grounds whatsoever.
Now, with respect to the allegation of adultery-and it is in this respect that I should like to give some pertinent detailed references in the evidence itself if I am permitted to do so-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the hon. member proceeds, I am concerned with the propriety of any detailed discussion of the evidence on second reading. The matter before the house is the principle of the bill, which is to dissolve the marriage of these people. The hon. member is, I think, within his rights in drawing the attention of the house to the fact
[Mr. Howard.!
that the principle should not be endorsed by the house because there are three defects, or three variations from the normal practice of the house in granting divorce by act of parliament. But when it comes to proving or substantiating these matters in detail it would seem to me that the proper place to do that would be in committee. I think the hon. member can make his point if he has any doubt about the proof of adultery but not to discuss the evidence in detail here.

Mr. Speaker, if I gave an indication to you that that was what I was trying to do, it is not the point which I was leading up to. I have no quarrel at this stage -as you have indicated perhaps I should have -with whether adultery had been committed and whether, following the practice of this house and of the other place, there is sufficient ground to dissolve the marriage. I have reference to the evidence produced before the committee in the other place but no reference to the question of whether adultery had or had not taken place.
My reference is to an entirely different matter and I hope to found upon this particular reference which I wish to make, which involves civil and human rights, a motion which would indicate that this house should not at this time consider second reading until another body has had an opportunity to consider this other matter. That is what I was leading toward and that is what I hope to make reference to by referring to the evidence itself. Therefore, if I may I should like to refer to page 14 of the evidence. This is the evidence by Mr. George Roland Foucher, age 43, who resides in Montreal. His occupation is an investigator. He appeared as a witness on behalf of the petitioner. He was sworn and testified as follows. I will paraphrase it. They went to a particular place and there they found certain things. If I can specify it, I should like to read from page 14 as follows: He made reference to the respondent and corespondent and said:
They had been in for over a couple of hours- we moved to the door and after knocking on it, the subject himself came to the door and opened it partly. I pushed on the door and we both rushed in and were met by a loud yell of pain inside, and just as we looked behind the door Mr.-was sitting in a wicker chair holding onto his foot. Our reaction was to ask him what happened-
I submit this is the normal reaction of someone who bursts into your premises. He found this man holding his foot. In any event, he followed the normal procedure and asked what happened. I continue:
-and he said that by pushing the door open I had knocked on his foot and he had a couple of broken toes.

It is not clear to me whether he had a couple of broken toes before and this action had injured them further, or whether he had a couple of broken toes as a result of the door being pushed open.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not clear that I follow the point of the evidence in relation to the second reading of the bill. I am not sure what the hon. member's argument is with respect to approving the principle of the granting of this divorce. If he is able to state it I wish he would. If he is not, I suggest he leave the reading of the evidence to when we are in committee.

I think perhaps I shall be able to show that without any difficulty, Mr. Speaker. This is what I was leading up to in that slight reference. Let me indicate to you in a general way what I was trying to do. I think perhaps I have proceeded far enough with the reading of the evidence about people pushing the door open and knocking on someone's toes and either breaking them or injuring them additionally where they had been broken. The witness then goes on to say that the man in question was more concerned about his foot than talking to them about the purpose of their visit which, I submit, is a perfectly reasonable thing to expect. The point I am leading to, is that this invasion of the privileges and rights, human rights, civil rights and civil liberties of that person should not be condoned and that a person should not have his premises invaded arbitrarily, such as was done here.
What I am submitting is that before this house proceeds to give second reading to this bill we might properly refer the subject matter thereof to another body established under authority of this parliament, an authority which deals in the field of litigation, deals in the field of human and civil rights, an organization for which all of us have respect and admiration in Canada. I suggest the subject matter of this bill should be referred to that group in order that we may ask that group to pass upon not only what I have read here so far but upon other factors which are substantiated in the evidence and with which I do not intend to deal at this time. I think this matter should be referred to that other body so that they may take cognizance of it and determine whether or not civil rights and human rights, the right of an individual to privacy, have or have not been invaded.
Don't be a hypocrite. You are destroying their rights in this house.
Mr. Speaker-

Hypocrisy.

It is not my intention to be drawn into a side discussion by those to whom I have referred as preferring to talk from their seats rather than from their places in the house. If my hon. friend, whoever it was, down in that corner wishes to make reference to hypocrites I suggest to him with all deference, with all due respect-and I am only assuming that it was the hon. member for Halifax-

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, it was the member for Halifax who has put up with a great deal of nonsense from that particular corner and who is glad he is far removed from it so he cannot smell the odour from it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Halifax is taking liberties which he should not take in this chamber in using offensive language to the hon. member who has the floor.
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to complain about the reference of the hon. member for Halifax to hypocrisy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will not proceed with that subject.

No; I do not ask him to withdraw. This is one thing I do not want to do. If the hon. member for Halifax wants to make those allegations and stand by them, that is his privilege, especially if he wants to make them by hiding behind his privileges and remaining in his seat.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member is speaking on a question of privilege he may do so. If he is speaking on second reading I wish he would proceed.
The hon. member for Halifax raised a question of privilege. This is what I was dealing with.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I thought that was disposed of.

If you have disposed of it, then I appreciate the manner in which you have done so. It was done in such a delicate way that there is no escape from it. The reference I am making to the evidence has to do with whether the rights of individuals to liberty, the rights of individuals to have their domicile, whether it be a home they own or a hotel or motel room they rent for the night, free from invasion, are to be protected. I say that we should refer to another body which has had considerable experience in this field the question of whether or not these human and civil rights have been invaded and ask that body to give an opinion to the house on the basis of their study and consideration of the matter. That is all I was leading up to and that is

Private Bills-Divorce
why I referred to the particular part of the evidence which I recited. On that basis I would therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):
That this bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada for examination and report thereon.

Mr. Speaker, before the motion is put I wish to argue, and I think I can do so effectively, that the amendment is clearly out of order in that it is not within the competence of the house to pass upon such a question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would be very appreciative of any assistance which can be given by the hon. member for Halifax on the question whether or not there is provision for reference of a question of this kind by the House of Commons to the Supreme Court of Canada and for the Supreme Court of Canada to receive such a reference and deal with it. If the amendment would be nugatory in the sense that it could not be carried out, then I would think its regularity might be questioned.

Mr. Speaker, that was
exactly the point I was going to raise. If such a motion were sent to the Supreme Court of Canada their lordships would hardly know how to deal with it. It would not come to them in any regular fashion or through any regular process of law. I can understand that my hon. friend has perhaps got himself into this difficulty because he does not understand what the ordinary process of law means.
With respect to the bruised or broken toes of the respondent's husband, a remedy was clearly available in the courts. If he had wished to do so he could have taken the matter into the police court and charged Foucher and his associate with trespass or with having occasioned him bodily harm. He had these remedies open to him. But I know of no authority whereby a reference can be made to the Supreme Court of Canada when no grounds are stated but merely a general opinion is sought. Surely the highest court in the land should not be burdened with dealing with a matter with respect to which rights already exist under the law if the respondent had wished to pursue them. According to the evidence, he did not choose to do so and I cannot see any point in the hon. member trying to protect somebody who did not try to protect himself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If I may interrupt the hon. member, perhaps he will have given consideration to whether there is any authority or precedent for a reference by the House of Commons to the Supreme Court of Canada

for advice on any matter and whether there is any power in the Supreme Court of Canada to receive and deal with such a reference.

I think that would require reference to the act which sets up the Supreme Court of Canada. If that were done a definite answer could probably be given to your question. However, I submit that the burden surely must rest on those who propound such an amendment to show that this is a proper course of action, and no attempt has been made to do that.

If I may speak on the point of order, Mr. Speaker, raised by the hon. member for Halifax, I should like to point out to him that it is completely irrelevant whether the respondent took any action or chose not to do so. The last point mentioned by the hon. member, whether or not we have the authority to take such a course, is the one to which we should address ourselves. As suggested by the hon. member for Halifax, I should like to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a statute passed by this house, being an act respecting the Supreme Court of Canada, chapter 259 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, which was amended by chapter 48 of the statutes of 1956, although the amendment is not relevant to this matter. I refer Your Honour to section 56 of the Supreme Court Act, this being the short title, which reads as follows:
The court-
The definition section indicates what the court is.
-or any two judges thereof, shall examine and report upon any private bill-
Of which this is one.
-or petition for a private bill-
There is a petition attached in this instance.
-presented to the Senate or House of Commons, and referred to the court under any rules or orders made by the Senate or House of Commons.
I submit that the House of Commons and the Senate together determined by enacting section 56 that under this section any private bill or petition for a private bill presented to the Senate or the House of Commons may be referred to the court under any rules or orders made by the Senate or House of Commons. I think there are perhaps no rules so far as the House of Commons are concerned. To my knowledge this has not occurred before. As there are no rules, we must look to the question of orders. If the house passes an order such as that to which I have alluded the matter would be referred to the Supreme

Court of Canada for its consideration and report thereon. I submit that the amendment is entirely in order pursuant to section 56 of the Supreme Court Act.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the section read by the hon. member for Skeena clearly indicates that the amendment he has placed before the house is quite out of order. As I heard it read, section 56 suggests that there is a right in the Supreme Court of Canada but the Supreme Court of Canada is a statutory court created by the parliament of Canada and only has jurisdiction to deal with such cases and such matters by way of petition or otherwise as come clearly within the four corners of the act itself. There is no right in the court as of right unless the statute itself says that these matters may be brought before the court.
The section to which the hon. member referred only deals with such petitions or private bills as come within our rules. I have looked through the rules and I am sure there is no rule in our standing orders making any such provision. If I am wrong, perhaps the hon. member might refer me to it. I am relying on my memory but so far as I can recall there is no rule in our standing orders which makes provision for the transmitting of any petition or private bill directly from this house to the Supreme Court of Canada. I think the provision in the act says in effect that if we should choose to establish a rule then the Supreme Court of Canada can and would be bound to hear the matter, but in the absence of such a rule the amendment is clearly out of order.

should like to speak to the point of order. If the hon. member was a member of the house committee last session-I do not recall whether or not he was-he would remember that this same problem arose at that time with regard to whether a committee had the power to come before the house and ask the house to make a motion to the effect that the attorney general investigate certain matters. We had before us then a precedent-I have not got the citation with me and I cannot remember the precise information-to the effect that the only request the house could make of the attorney general, or in this case the supreme court, would be one which related to something which happened before the committee itself, that is if there were perjury in the evidence or some offence committed before a committee of the house.
Here we have a motion based on an allegation connected with an investigation of some incident that happened outside of the house in one of the provinces of this country.

I think, on the face of it-

No,

Perhaps I could clear that up before we go on.

speechtext: Order; I will hear the hon. member later.

In so far as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) is concerned, as I understood his remarks he said that we have the right to refer matters to the Supreme Court of Canada only if there are rules. I would point out that the Supreme Court Act is not specific. It is not a specific reference under the rules, but it says, refer to the court under any rules or orders. I submit that if the house has the motion properly before it, and if it deems it wise to pass the motion, then it becomes an order of reference to the supreme court. We have no rules, there is no specific rule and because the wording of that section is general, we then consider it under the item of orders. I submit that if there were rules they would be the standing orders, I presume.
The section says that matters of this nature may be referred to the supreme court, and if there were rules they would set up this procedure for referring such matters to the supreme court, and the manner in which that could be done. The Supreme Court Act is general and refers to any rules. Since we have no rules I submit we are at liberty to hold that the motion is in order because it falls under the classification of orders. If the

motion were passed, it would then be an order of the house for a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena has submitted an amendment which raises a point which is rather novel in that it suggests a reference of the subject matter of this bill to the Supreme Court of Canada, an action for which there is no precedent as I am advised, although there are precedents for such action being taken by the Senate which appears to have established a procedure for so doing. The section of the act under which this reference is sought to be made provides that the court or any two of the judges thereof shall examine and report upon any private bill or petition for a private bill presented to the Senate or the House of Commons. The amendment seeks to refer the subject matter of this bill, and not the bill itself. I think in that sense the motion is defective.
The other point which was raised was that the section of the Supreme Court Act to which I referred goes on to say that the matter must be referred to the court under rules or orders made by the Senate or House of Commons. The point is made; "what is meant is rules or standing orders," and that is met by the argument of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) that an order of the house would come within the section, an order referring this matter would be an order within the meaning of that section of the act. I rather think that the other opinion is the better one because rules and orders are referred to in the plural and as synonymous. Our orders are called standing orders, and if the House of Commons chose to use this machinery for a reference to the supreme court, presumably they would have established standing orders by which the reference could be made, which we have not done.
However, I have some doubt on that point and if the matter turned on that point I would prefer to reserve it and give consideration to it. Since the amendment as submitted seems not to come within the section on rather narrow grounds, namely that the reference must be of a private bill or petition, not of the subject matter thereof, I rule the amendment out of order.
Mr. Speaker, it is-

I may with your leave, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin), the motion that has been moved except that I should like to amend it by putting in the words "this bill", where the words "the subject matter of this bill" are now.
